common_name: Big Blue Sea Holly (Large-Flowered Steel-Blue Eryngium)

planting.note: Transplant divisions or started plants in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Big Blue is a selection of flat sea holly chosen for extra-large, intensely steel-blue flower heads and bracts.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, even sandy or rocky soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces floppy, short-lived growth in this drought-loving perennial. Big Blue bears branching stems topped with thistle-like, metallic steel-blue flower heads surrounded by spiny, equally blue bracts from midsummer into fall, larger and more intensely colored than the species, and the whole plant takes on a silvery-blue cast that makes it a striking accent among softer-textured perennials and grasses. Established plants develop a long taproot that makes them extremely drought-tolerant but resentful of transplanting or division, so site it thoughtfully the first time. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers heavily, and the dried flower heads hold their color well for cutting and winter arrangements; leave some stems standing through winter for texture and seed for goldfinches.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Hummelo Betony (Dense-Spiked Purple Perennial Plant of the Year)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Hummelo was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 2019 for its exceptionally long, tidy bloom and clean habit.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Hummelo tolerates more moisture and heavier soil than many gray-leaved Mediterranean herbs in the mint family. Popularized by Dutch designer Piet Oudolf and named the Perennial Plant Association's 2019 Perennial Plant of the Year, it forms a neat, low mound of crinkled green foliage that stays attractive all season, sending up dense, upright spikes of rosy-purple flowers held well above the leaves from early to late summer, a much longer and tidier bloom period than older betony selections. Bees work the flowers steadily, and the sterile-ish, low-seed habit means it spreads slowly by clump rather than seeding around aggressively. Cut back after the main flush for a possible rebloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Montrose White was selected by nurserywoman Nancy Goodwin at Montrose Gardens in North Carolina for denser habit and heavier bloom than the species.

directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this tough, drought-tolerant mint relative shrugs off heat and humidity far better than most white-flowered perennials, making it a Gulf South mainstay. Montrose White forms a dense, rounded mound of small, aromatic, mint-scented leaves smothered from midsummer into fall in a haze of tiny, pure white, two-lipped flowers that draw bees and small butterflies in great numbers, functioning almost like a perennial baby's breath in the border. It self-seeds modestly but is easy to edit, and shearing the whole plant back by half after the first flush of bloom encourages denser regrowth and a second wave of flowers into autumn. Established plants need little supplemental water and rarely need dividing, staying attractive for years with only an annual spring cleanup of old stems.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cat's Meow is a more compact, tidier-habited sport of the popular Walker's Low catmint, fitting smaller borders and edging.

directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; catmint rots quickly in wet, heavy soil over winter, so good drainage matters more than fertility. Cat's Meow arose as a more compact, upright, and floriferous sport of the widely grown Walker's Low, covering itself in short spikes of lavender-blue flowers over gray-green, aromatic foliage from late spring through summer, with a shearing after the first flush reliably triggering a strong second bloom into fall. Its tighter, rounder habit holds up better without flopping than older, looser catmints, making it useful for edging paths and border fronts where Walker's Low would sprawl too wide. Extremely drought-tolerant once established and generally ignored by deer and rabbits, it needs only an annual spring cutback to remove old growth before new shoots emerge.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Mount Everest Allium (Giant White Ornamental Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Mount Everest produces one of the largest pure white flower globes among ornamental onions, often 6-8 inches across.

directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep and 10-14 inches apart in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun; standing water around the bulbs in winter causes rot. Mount Everest sends up a tall, sturdy, leafless stem in late spring topped by a dense, perfectly round globe of small starry white flowers that can reach 6 to 8 inches across, one of the largest and showiest white ornamental onions available, holding its form as a dramatic vertical accent in the border for several weeks. Like other large alliums, its strappy basal foliage yellows and dies back before or during bloom, so plant it behind or among later-emerging perennials that will mask the fading leaves. Deer- and rabbit-resistant and drought-tolerant once established, it multiplies slowly by offsets and is best left undisturbed for years, with the dried seed heads adding continued architectural interest into fall if left standing.
